strengths: Causal2Vec provides a clear, technically plausible approach to adapting decoder-only LLMs for embeddings: inject a compact bidirectional text representation and concatenate its final hidden state with the EOS representation. The method preserves the backbone’s causal attention and directly addresses a relevant NLP problem.

Evaluation covers 56 MTEB datasets, seven task categories, and three backbones. Improvements over LLM2Vec are consistent across backbones, and component ablations on 41 datasets support the practical usefulness of both contextual-token injection and concatenation.

The efficiency–quality tradeoff is attractive relative to methods that repeat input text or add demonstrations. Figure 2 shows substantially lower encoding latency than ECHO and few-shot bge-en-icl, with relatively small overhead over an ordinary LLM.

The manuscript supplies equations, checkpoint identifiers, training hyperparameters, dataset sources, instructions, and per-dataset results. These details make the core method reasonably reproducible and support a Findings-level empirical contribution.
weaknesses: The proposed explanations exceed the evidence. Improved aggregate scores do not establish that removing causal masks damages pretrained semantic knowledge, or that concatenation specifically mitigates recency bias. Controlled attention-mask comparisons and position-sensitive distractor experiments are absent. These claims should be qualified independently of the demonstrated performance gains.

The experiments do not fully distinguish contextual information flow from combining two embedding models and increasing output dimensionality. Concatenation doubles the representation size, but there is no dimension-matched comparison or simple E5–LLM concatenation baseline without contextual-token injection. Appendix C.2 retains injection in every variant, so it does not resolve this alternative explanation.

Several headline and ablation differences are small without uncertainty estimates. The default Mistral model scores 66.10 versus 66.08 for few-shot bge-en-icl and 65.87 for MGH; concatenation adds only 0.19 on MTEB-MINI for Mistral. Multiple seeds or paired uncertainty estimates would strengthen claims of superiority and conclusions drawn from similarly small placement/freezing differences. The ICL variant’s 66.85 is stronger evidence, but its efficiency must be evaluated separately.

The efficiency analysis omits downstream storage and similarity-search costs from doubled embeddings, and does not adequately document timing batch size, warm-up, synchronization, or tokenization coverage. The efficiency paragraph also quotes ordinary-LLM timings, such as 4.37 ms, where Figure 2 reports 4.70 ms for Causal2Vec. The substantial qualitative speed advantage remains credible, but the reported protocol and numerical comparisons need correction.

Reproduction and comparison details remain incomplete: hard-negative counts and selection, LoRA target modules, and the exact Causal2Vec ICL procedure are not specified. Publicly available training data alone does not ensure matched training conditions across baselines, especially when the method incorporates an already trained E5 encoder. These limitations, together with the unresolved mechanism and modest gains over the strongest comparators, limit the case for main-conference publication.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, technically plausible contribution: a bidirectional encoder supplies a contextual prefix to a causal LLM, and contextual/EOS representations are concatenated. The method addresses a relevant NLP problem while retaining the backbone’s causal attention.

Evaluation is substantial: 56 MTEB datasets across seven task categories and three backbones. Improvements over LLM2Vec are consistent, ranging from 0.78 to 1.30 average points. The controlled ablations also support modest gains over ordinary causal last-token pooling.

The experiments examine both proposed components, encoder choice, encoder freezing, token placement, and token count. Public model identifiers, training hyperparameters, dataset sources, evaluation instructions, and per-dataset results provide a reasonable basis for reproduction.

The supported empirical contribution merits Findings: competitive embedding quality with substantially shorter LLM inputs than repetition- and demonstration-based alternatives. This recommendation rests on the demonstrated method and results, rather than the stronger mechanistic explanations.
weaknesses: The proposed mechanisms are insufficiently established. Comparisons with other methods do not isolate whether bidirectional attention damages pretrained semantic knowledge, and no controlled positional-noise or length-based experiment directly tests reduced recency bias. A matched causal-versus-bidirectional comparison within the same framework would strengthen these claims.

The experiments do not fully distinguish contextual information flow from combining two complementary embedding models. Table 10’s Bi-EOS alternative still injects the contextual token into the LLM. A simple encoder/LLM concatenation baseline without prefix injection, together with a matched-output-dimension control, would better isolate the contribution.

Several distinctions are too small to interpret confidently without variability estimates. The default model scores 66.10 versus 66.08 for few-shot bge-en-icl, while several design ablations differ by only 0.09–0.19 points. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported. The evidence supports competitiveness more strongly than decisive superiority or necessity of every design choice.

Efficiency reporting needs qualification. Section 4.4 uses the plain LLM’s timing values when calculating Causal2Vec’s advertised savings; Figure 2 reports 4.70 ms for Causal2Vec versus the cited 4.37 ms. The approach also doubles embedding dimensionality, but index storage and similarity-search costs are not evaluated. The 66.85 best score uses ICL and should be clearly separated from the default model’s efficiency advantages.

Comparison and reproducibility details remain incomplete. The public-retrieval-data restriction does not establish matched training histories, especially with an additional pretrained E5 encoder. Hard-negative construction, LoRA target modules, and timing batch/padding settings are not sufficiently specified. These issues, together with overstated mechanistic conclusions, limit the case for main-conference publication.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, practical contribution to text embedding: a compact bidirectional encoder supplies a contextual prefix to a causal LLM, and contextual/EOS concatenation provides the final representation. The method preserves the backbone’s causal attention and is straightforward to understand.

Evaluation covers 56 MTEB datasets and three backbones. Improvements over LLM2Vec are consistent: 0.78, 0.80, and 1.30 average points. These results support the practical usefulness of the approach beyond a single model or task.

The experimental analysis includes component ablations, alternative pooling methods, encoder choices, token positions, encoder freezing, and contextual-token counts. The appendix supplies model identifiers, substantial training details, instructions, and per-dataset results.

Figure 2 supports a useful encoding-efficiency advantage over ECHO and few-shot bge-en-icl, with latency close to a standard LLM. Taken together, the empirical results support a contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Benchmark improvements do not establish that bidirectional attention damages pretrained semantic knowledge or that contextual/EOS concatenation mitigates recency bias. Controlled attention-mask comparisons and positional-noise experiments would be needed to substantiate these explanations.

The ablations do not fully distinguish contextual conditioning from combining complementary encoders. Table 10’s Bi-EOS baseline still injects the contextual token into the LLM. A baseline concatenating independently computed E5 and standard LLM embeddings, with comparable training and output dimensions, would better isolate the proposed interaction. The weaker standalone E5 results do not exclude an ensemble explanation.

Several decisive margins are small and have no uncertainty estimates. The default model scores 66.10 versus 66.08 for few-shot bge-en-icl; several design choices differ by only 0.1–0.3 points. The ICL variant reaches 66.85, but its efficiency is not reported. Thus, the evidence supports competitive performance more clearly than a robust state-of-the-art advantage.

The efficiency account is incomplete. Concatenation doubles embedding dimensionality, increasing vector storage and similarity-search costs, which are not measured. Timing batch sizes, warm-up, and inclusion of tokenization are unspecified. The efficiency paragraph also mistakenly uses standard-LLM measurements, such as 4.37 ms, instead of Causal2Vec’s 4.70 ms. This does not erase the speedup but warrants correction.

Comparison and reproduction details need clarification. The public-retrieval-only framing should explicitly account for E5’s prior embedding training and the inclusion of NLI in the training mixture; unseen-task generalization cannot be inferred solely from the current fine-tuning labels. The manuscript also leaves hard-negative sampling details, LoRA target modules, and the exact ICL example-selection procedure insufficiently specified. These limitations, together with the unresolved attribution of gains, prevent a main-conference recommendation.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, technically coherent approach to improving decoder-based embeddings: a bidirectional encoder supplies a contextual prefix, and concatenating its final hidden state with the EOS representation provides complementary information. The method is directly relevant to NLP representation learning and retrieval.

Evaluation covers all 56 English MTEB datasets and four backbones spanning 1.3B–7B parameters. Improvements across these backbones support the method’s usefulness beyond a single model. Table 2 provides particularly useful controlled evidence: contextual-token injection improves both tested backbones, and concatenation provides additional gains.

The ablations are unusually comprehensive, covering encoder choice, encoder freezing, token count and placement, pooling, direct embedding concatenation, and attention mechanisms. These experiments substantiate the practical contribution even where the proposed mechanistic explanations remain uncertain.

Inference measurements demonstrate a useful efficiency advantage over input repetition and in-context examples, with relatively small overhead against the standard Mistral baseline. The appendices document model identifiers, training data, prompts, optimization settings, and per-dataset results sufficiently well to support reproduction of the core approach.
weaknesses: The evidence establishes a useful embedding method more convincingly than it establishes the proposed explanation about preserving pretrained semantic knowledge. Figure 3 changes pooling together with attention, comparing causal last-token pooling against bidirectional mean pooling. Table 15 offers a better control, but its small differences do not demonstrate semantic degradation or identify pretraining–finetuning mismatch as the cause. Claims that bidirectional conversion is generally unsuitable should be narrowed.

The headline state-of-the-art claim is statistically fragile for the default model: 66.10 versus 66.08 for bge-en-icl and 65.87 for MGH. Experiments use one fixed seed without uncertainty estimates. The ICL variant reaches a stronger 66.85, but introduces the extra input computation that motivates the default method. Furthermore, retrieval performance remains below bge-en-icl (57.28 versus 60.08), so the advantage is in the aggregate benchmark rather than across all task categories.

The recency-bias experiment is insufficiently specified and does not isolate the claimed mechanism. The noise source, length, sampling procedure, truncation behavior, and whether the bidirectional encoder receives the same corrupted text are unclear. Comparing the complete method only against the standard baseline cannot distinguish robustness from contextual-token injection versus concatenation. Noise at different positions and a contextual-token-only ablation would provide stronger evidence.

The comparison protocol should distinguish the current finetuning data from the additional training history inherited through the pretrained E5 encoder. Using the same retrieval mixture does not equalize all prior embedding supervision. This particularly limits the interpretation that non-retrieval results establish generalization to previously unseen task types; it does not by itself invalidate the observed benchmark gains.

Some practical claims exceed the measurements. Concatenation doubles embedding dimensionality, and the small-corpus end-to-end timings in Table 13 do not characterize large-index memory or search costs. The efficiency paragraph also quotes standard-LLM timings rather than Causal2Vec timings for its examples. Several experimental variants, especially ICL and noise evaluation, need more implementation detail. Overall, the core empirical contribution supports Findings, while these limitations and the modest, uncertain advantage over the strongest alternatives limit the case for main-conference publication.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, technically plausible contribution: a bidirectional encoder supplies a contextual prefix to a causal LLM, and contextual-token/EOS concatenation produces the final embedding. The method is directly relevant to NLP representation learning and retrieval.

The empirical evaluation is substantial: 56 MTEB datasets spanning seven task categories and four LLM backbones. Improvements across backbones support the practical usefulness of the approach beyond a single favorable model.

The ablations meaningfully support the architectural contribution. Table 2 separates the benefits of contextual-token injection and concatenation; Table 4 compares against direct embedding fusion; additional experiments examine encoder choice, pooling, token placement, and attention direction. These establish more than an isolated benchmark improvement.

The inference measurements demonstrate a useful quality–latency tradeoff relative to methods that repeat inputs or add demonstrations. The appendices provide model identifiers, training hyperparameters, dataset composition, prompts, and per-dataset results, making the core approach reasonably reproducible. Overall, the supported empirical contribution merits Findings, although the stronger explanatory claims do not warrant a clear main-conference recommendation.
weaknesses: The attention-mismatch explanation is not established. Figure 3 compares causal attention with last-token pooling against bidirectional attention with mean pooling, confounding attention direction with representation extraction. Table 15 provides a more controlled comparison within Causal2Vec, but its small differences do not demonstrate loss of pretrained semantic knowledge or establish that bidirectional conversion is generally unsuitable. These conclusions should be narrowed to the tested configurations.

The headline state-of-the-art claim needs statistical qualification. Without ICL, the Mistral result exceeds bge-en-icl by only 0.02 points and MGH by 0.23 points. The paper reports one fixed training seed without uncertainty estimates; fixing a seed does not establish that these differences are reliable. The larger cross-backbone gains and ICL result are more persuasive than the precise leaderboard ranking.

The recency-bias experiment is insufficiently specified and does not isolate the claimed mechanism. The source, length, and sampling of appended noise are unspecified, as is whether the auxiliary encoder receives the same corrupted text. Table 3 compares the complete method against a baseline, so it cannot attribute improved robustness specifically to concatenation. Matched corruption for both encoders, position-controlled noise, and component-level robustness ablations would strengthen this claim.

The efficiency conclusions extend beyond the measurements. The method doubles embedding dimensionality, increasing index storage and similarity-search costs. Appendix Table 13 measures total completion time on three small retrieval datasets, where encoding can dominate; it does not establish negligible overhead for large precomputed indexes. Also, the main text incorrectly uses the standard-LLM timings of 4.37/6.50 ms when describing Causal2Vec, whose plotted timings are 4.70/7.00 ms.

Some details limit the precision of the comparisons and reproducibility. The contribution of E5's prior embedding training should be distinguished from the shared retrieval fine-tuning data when describing data fairness. Hard-negative configuration, the direct-fusion baseline's training and normalization, and the exact ICL setup deserve fuller specification. Backbone-specific encoder-freezing decisions are justified using MTEB-MINI results without clearly separating model selection from final evaluation.

strengths: The paper offers a clear, practical contribution to text representation learning: a compact contextual prefix supplies whole-input information while preserving the decoder’s causal attention. The method is straightforward to implement and relevant to retrieval and other NLP applications.

Evaluation is broad: 56 MTEB datasets across seven task categories and four backbones. Improvements across architectures support the method’s usefulness beyond a single model. Mistral-7B reaches 66.10 overall, and adding ICL raises this to 66.85.

The ablations substantiate both proposed components. In Table 2, contextual-token insertion improves performance on both tested backbones, and concatenating contextual and EOS representations adds further gains. Comparisons with direct embedding concatenation, alternative pooling strategies, different encoders, and token counts strengthen the empirical contribution.

Measured inference times demonstrate a useful quality–latency tradeoff against methods that repeat inputs or add demonstrations. The non-ICL variant approximately matches bge-en-icl’s overall accuracy with substantially lower encoding latency.

The presentation and appendices provide substantial reproduction detail, including model identifiers, training data composition, optimization settings, instructions, and per-dataset results. Overall, the empirical contribution supports acceptance at least in Findings; the practical benefits make main-conference consideration plausible.
weaknesses: The strongest headline gains are small relative to uncertainty that is not measured. The non-ICL model exceeds bge-en-icl by only 0.02 points and MGH by 0.23 points. A single fixed seed does not establish the reliability of these differences. The 0.77-point ICL improvement is more persuasive, but repeated runs would strengthen the state-of-the-art claim.

The explanation that bidirectional conversion damages pretrained semantic knowledge is not directly established. Figure 3 changes both attention and pooling, confounding their effects. Table 15 supplies additional evidence within Causal2Vec, but its small differences do not isolate the proposed mechanism or establish a general disadvantage of bidirectional adaptation.

The recency-bias experiment is insufficiently specified and controlled. The source and length of appended noise, truncation behavior, and whether the bidirectional encoder receives the same corrupted text are unclear. Without these details and a contextual-token-only ablation under noise, Table 3 cannot cleanly attribute robustness to the proposed concatenation mechanism.

The matched-data framing should explicitly account for the pretrained E5 encoder’s embedding-specific training history. Matching the subsequent retrieval fine-tuning data does not establish matched prior supervision. This does not invalidate the practical method, but it qualifies claims that improvements isolate architecture under equivalent training resources.

Efficiency evidence concerns primarily encoding latency. Concatenation doubles embedding dimensionality, affecting corpus storage and similarity-search costs; Table 13’s small end-to-end benchmarks do not settle large-index deployment costs. The 66.85 ICL result also should remain clearly separated from the non-ICL latency advantage. These limitations, together with the uncertain margins and stronger-than-supported mechanistic interpretation, make my main-conference recommendation borderline.
